rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Sulphuric acid earns "king of chemicals" by doing three jobs. As a **strong dibasic acid** (dilute) it etches metals below hydrogen (**Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂**), dissolves oxides and carbonates, and — being **non-volatile (bp 338 °C)** — displaces the volatile acids HCl, HF and HNO₃ from their salts.…

rows.text: ***The sugar snake*** - pour concentrated H2SO4 onto table sugar and a steaming black column grows from the beaker: the acid has stripped 11 waters per 12 carbons out of sucrose, leaving pure carbon scaffold.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The King of Chemicals H₂SO₄ — "king of chemicals" — as acid, oxidant and dehydrating agent, plus its uses. Its three personalities and the safety they demand.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 As an acid - Strong **dibasic** acid: ionises in two steps (H₂SO₄ → H⁺ + HSO₄⁻ fully; HSO₄⁻ → H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ fairly); dense oily liquid ("oil of vitriol"), non-volatile (bp 338 °C). - Normal acid reactions: metals below H (Zn + H₂SO₄(dil) → ZnSO₄ + H₂), bases/oxides (CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O), carbonates (Na₂CO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + CO₂ + H₂O).…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Dil: H2 with Zn; no Cu reaction. Conc hot: SO2 with Cu/C/S/HBr. Dehydrant: sugar -> C, HCOOH -> CO, ethanol -> ethene. Non-volatile: makes HCl/HF/HNO3. Bp 338 C. Add acid to water!

rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): Describe sulphuric acid as (a) an acid, (b) an oxidising agent, and (c) a dehydrating agent, with one equation each.** — **(a) Acid:** dilute H₂SO₄ is a strong **dibasic** acid: **Zn + H₂SO₄(dil) → ZnSO₄ + H₂↑** (also neutralises bases: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O; liberates CO₂ from carbonates).…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): Why is concentrated H2SO4 used to prepare HCl from NaCl but not HBr from KBr?** — With NaCl the reaction is simple **non-volatile-acid displacement**: **NaCl + H₂SO₄(conc) → NaHSO₄ + HCl↑** — chloride is too weak a reducer to be oxidised, so clean HCl distils off.…

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Concentration is the switch: dilute H2SO4 is just a strong acid whose only oxidant is H+, while hot concentrated H2SO4 - still largely molecular - grabs electrons itself and is reduced to SO2; the same liquid, two personalities chosen by dilution.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: H2SO4 "king of chemicals": strong dibasic acid (sulphate + hydrogensulphate salts), dense oily non-volatile liquid (bp 338 C). ACID: Zn + H2SO4(dil) -> ZnSO4 + H2; CuO + H2SO4 -> CuSO4 + H2O; Na2CO3 -> CO2. NON-VOLATILE DISPLACER: NaCl + H2SO4(conc) -> NaHSO4 + HCl; CaF2 -> HF; KNO3 -> HNO3.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Sulphuric acid production per capita was long used as an index of a country's industrial maturity - the king of chemicals crowns economies.

Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **Dibasic acid** | Two replaceable H⁺ | sulphate + hydrogensulphate salts | | **Non-volatile acid** | Low vapour pressure, high bp (338 °C) | displaces HCl, HNO₃ | | **Dehydrating agent** | Removes H and O as water from compounds | sugar → carbon | | **Charring** | Dehydration leaving carbon |…  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why concentrated H₂SO₄ oxidises but dilute does not - The oxidising species is the **molecule itself** (S at +6 with strongly bound water): hot concentrated H₂SO₄ accepts electrons, being reduced to SO₂. In dilute solution the molecule is fully ionised — only H⁺ remains as a (weak) oxidant, giving H₂ with active metals.…  ·  ## 5. Comparison Tables | Behaviour | dilute H₂SO₄ | conc. H₂SO₄ | |---|---|---| | Acid strength | strong, ionised | largely molecular | | Oxidising | no (H⁺ only) | yes (→ SO₂) | | With Cu | no reaction | CuSO₄ + SO₂ | | With Zn | ZnSO₄ + H₂ | ZnSO₄ + SO₂ | | Dehydrating | no | yes (sugar → C) | | Drying gases | no | yes (hygroscopic) |

rows.text: State the safety rule for diluting H2SO4 and explain it.  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions - **"H₂SO₄ always oxidises."** Only hot concentrated acid; dilute acid behaves as a normal strong acid (H₂ with Zn). - **"It dehydrates by absorbing water molecules only."** It removes the *elements* of water (H and O) from compounds like sugar and formic acid that contain no water at all.…  ·  ## 7. Exam Application - Three-personality structure: acid / oxidant / dehydrant, one equation each. - The sugar-charcoal equation is the dehydrating signature. - Safety: acid-to-water rule with the heat argument.
